F1.claim: the exhibit's own kind: an exhibit of Columbia's Rare Book & Manuscript Library
F1.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F2.quote: The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence is a collaboration between the Columbia English Department, the Columbia University Rare Books & Manuscript Library, and Columbia University’s Digital Scholarship department.
F2.claim: the exhibit's makers: three Columbia units in collaboration
F2.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F3.quote: This exhibition explores the long, shared history of literature and computation through the Columbia Library’s holdings.
F3.claim: the exhibit's subject: the shared history of literature and computation, through Columbia's holdings
F3.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F4.quote: We present texts that participate in early debates about whether writing was a skill to be honed or a gift to be appreciated and whether the skills of writing could be learned and even made into repeatable algorithms.
F4.claim: what it presents: texts in early debates over writing as skill or gift, learnable and made into repeatable algorithms
F4.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F5.quote: Is writing like any other craft that can be learned and taught?
F5.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F6.quote: Following a timeline from circa 1890–1970, this exhibition explores professional manuals, devices, and techniques that promised to make writing easier—and even to automate it.
F6.claim: its timeline, circa 1890–1970, and its objects: manuals, devices and techniques that promised to ease or automate writing
F6.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F7.quote: The Literary History of AI showcases examples of algorithmic composition, such as prose and poetry written by machines, alongside literature written with the aid of algorithmic and combinatorial devices.
F7.claim: what it shows: algorithmic composition (prose and poetry written by machines) beside literature written with algorithmic and combinatorial devices
F7.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F8.quote: This exhibition broadly tracks two broad stories related to the literary history of AI: production and analysis.
F8.claim: its two stories: production and analysis
F8.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F9.quote: AI & Literary Production: Romance, Mystery, and Defense Aeronautics
F9.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F10.quote: The first story follows experiments in the genesis of literature as a professional and technical craft, facilitated by writing manuals, guides for churning out mystery or romance plots, such as Wycliffe Hill’s Plot Genies, and plot generators such as William Wallace Cook’s Plotto series.
F10.claim: the first story: literature as professional and technical craft, through writing manuals, Hill's Plot Genies and Cook's Plotto
F10.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F11.quote: Automated text generation catalyzed a wave of early 20th-century patents, from Arthur Blanchard’s “movie-writer” machine and Henrietta Rose Montague’s “name selector.”
F11.claim: automated text generation catalyzed early 20th-century patents (Blanchard's 'movie-writer', Montague's 'name selector')
F11.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F12.quote: Some how-to manuals incorporated simple plot generators, with spinning devices or automatic number generators that would guide would-be novelists past writers’ block.
F12.claim: how-to manuals with simple plot generators, spinning devices or number generators
F12.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F13.quote: We follow these professional how-to manuals into mid-twentieth century computer experimentation in algorithmic and automated writing, from Christopher Strachey, who wrote a love letter program in the 1940s, to Margaret Masterman, a linguist who pioneered the use of computers to aid automatic translation.
F13.claim: from the manuals to mid-century computer experiments in algorithmic writing: Strachey's 1940s love letter program, Masterman's computer-aided translation
F13.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F14.quote: The mid 20th-century saw an existential question arise as to whether programs should be written based on frames or grammar, a divide that drew much of its vocabulary from comparing literary genres to linguistic rules.
F14.claim: the mid-century question of frames or grammar, its vocabulary drawn from literary genre against linguistic rule
F14.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F15.quote: Were situational specifics or universal linguistic structures the better way to teach text-generating computers to write?
F15.claim: the question put as situational specifics or universal structures for text-generating computers
F15.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F16.quote: This debate would influence early experiments with chat bots, baseball analytics, defense training programs, and match-making algorithms.
F16.claim: the debate's influence on early chat bots, baseball analytics, defense training and match-making algorithms
F16.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F17.quote: The Literary History of AI showcases how early 20th-century popular texts for aspiring screenplay writers, romance novelists, and pulp fictioneers influence and shape contemporary, machine learning-based tools used in automating aviation accident reports and defense logistics.
F17.claim: the exhibit's line to the present: early popular writing texts influence and shape machine learning-based tools for aviation accident reports and defense logistics
F17.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F18.quote: AI & Literary Analysis: Character types, story pieces, chat bots, and medical care
F18.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F19.quote: The second story tracks the use of algorithms to analyze literature, highlighting works such as Columbia alumna Harriot Fansler’s dissection of Types of Prose Narratives, which she called a “textbook for the story writer” to Georges Polti’s Les trente-six situations dramatiques (1895), which categorized what he theorized were the 36 timeless situations that structured human experience, from vengeance and retribution to love and sacrifice.
F19.claim: the second story: algorithms to analyze literature, from Fansler's Types of Prose Narratives to Polti's thirty-six situations (1895)
F19.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F20.quote: This section of the exhibition includes analyses and compendia of folk tales, diagrams of plot structures, including Harry Stephen Keeler’s “web-word” designs, and Carolyn Well’s distillation of the mystery novel.
F20.claim: its analyses and compendia: folk tales, plot diagrams (Keeler's 'web-word'), Carolyn Well's distillation of the mystery novel
F20.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F21.quote: The interest in narrative analysis and plot visualization also catalyzed the development of new techniques for organizing story elements.
F21.claim: narrative analysis catalyzed techniques for organizing story elements
F21.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F22.quote: Databases, scrapbooks, and notecards forecast zettelkasten, Evernote, and Google Docs.
F22.claim: databases, scrapbooks and notecards forecast zettelkasten, Evernote and Google Docs
F22.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F23.quote: Information storage was increasingly understood to be central both to analysis and to composition.
F23.claim: information storage understood as central to analysis and composition
F23.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F24.quote: These materials illustrate how early twentieth-century techniques used to generate prose were paralleled by advances in natural language processing, which today animate narratively “intelligent” bots such as Apple’s Siri and Amazon’s Alexa , as well as influence interactive and automated forms of medical diagnostics.
F24.claim: early techniques to generate prose paralleled by natural language processing, which animates Siri and Alexa and influences automated medical diagnostics
F24.date: the exhibit's about page, '© Copyright 2022', census copy read 2026-11-01

F25.claim: the exhibit is arranged in eight cases (Case No. 1 to Case No. 8), with a credits page
